issue: Built on the most generous reading, the decorrelation mechanism is real and rule 5 is largely correct: commit-and-reveal isolation genuinely removes the induced inter-agent herding (information-cascade / anchoring) that would otherwise make sequential same-model reviews collapse toward the first opinion. That defense holds and I affirm it. What does NOT survive the steelman is the single word 'only' combined with 'more than N correlated draws'. Isolation removes *induced* correlation (from peer exposure); it cannot remove *shared-prior* correlation (every seat is the same model class drawing on the same training distribution). So isolation is necessary but not sufficient to make the fleet 'more than N correlated draws' -- the residual shared-blind-spot correlation persists. The paper's own LIMITATIONS states exactly this corrected position ('every seat is the same model class and can share a blind spot. A fleet's agreement is *not* independent corroboration'), so rule 5 as written is in direct internal tension with the manuscript's own honest concession. A reader who sees only rule 5 (the binding constitution every agent reads) would over-read the guarantee.
why_it_matters: Decorrelation is the load-bearing justification for running a large same-model fleet at all; if 'only ... makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws' is read literally, it overstates what the mechanism delivers and contradicts LIMITATIONS. Because rule 5 is the 'constitution' that overrides later prompts on conflict ('this file wins'), the overclaim sits in the highest-authority document, not a marketing blurb. The fix is nearly free and the correct claim already exists verbatim elsewhere in the manuscript.
proposed_fix: Soften 'the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws' to a precise, sufficiency-honest version, e.g. 'the thing that removes *induced* herding and makes the fleet more than N *sequentially anchored* draws -- residual shared-model correlation is addressed only by the optional cross-provider leg (see LIMITATIONS).' This aligns rule 5 with the manuscript's own LIMITATIONS concession (C-034) rather than introducing a new claim.
risk_of_fix: Low. The replacement asserts strictly less than the original and is already stated in LIMITATIONS, so it cannot make a correct passage wrong. Minor risk: over-hedging rule 5 could blunt the (legitimate) rhetorical force of commit-and-reveal as the core anti-herding control; keep the affirmative half ('removes induced herding') intact so the genuine contribution is not undersold.

location.section: README.md (where it fits / bet 2)

quote:
re-runs your analysis and hands back a corrected,
   reproducing manuscript
issue: This is one of the two headline 'bets' the paper rests its differentiation on (C-021), and it is stated as a present-tense capability the tool delivers ('hands back a corrected, reproducing manuscript'; the same sentence closes 'so you leave with a redline and a clean draft, not a to-do list'). But the paper's own LIMITATIONS.md says the opposite about exactly this capability: 'until that ships and is demonstrated end-to-end on a real paper, treat Act II as *designed, demonstrated in part* â€” and re-derive any number yourself before trusting it.' A capability that has, by the authors' own admission, never been demonstrated end-to-end on a real paper is being sold in the contribution paragraph as a finished, reproducing-manuscript-returning system. The word 'reproducing' is the load-bearing overclaim: LIMITATIONS concedes there is not even a precise reproduction predicate yet (no float tolerance / fixed seeds / environment capture defined). The hedge that would neutralize this lives in a different file, so the marketing surface and the limitations surface state contradictory things about the same headline claim.
why_it_matters: Per the locked rubric, a 'fatal framing/overclaim in which the stated contribution is not what the evidence supports' is a High. The stated contribution here ('hands back a corrected, reproducing manuscript') is precisely what the evidence (own LIMITATIONS) says is NOT yet demonstrated. A reader deciding whether to feed the tool their real data and code will reasonably believe the rebuild is a working, validated pipeline; it is a design that has never run end-to-end. This is the single claim most likely to cause a user to over-trust an unverified number in their own manuscript.
proposed_fix: Tense-match the claim to the evidence at the point of the claim. Replace the present-tense capability with a designed/partial framing, e.g. 'an integrated rebuild *designed* to re-run your analysis and hand back a corrected, reproducing manuscript (Act II is implemented but not yet demonstrated end-to-end on a real paper â€” see LIMITATIONS.md)'. Keep the aspiration; remove the implication that the reproducing rebuild is a finished, validated deliverable.
risk_of_fix: Softening the headline bet weakens the pitch's central differentiation and could read as the tool conceding it does less than competitors; the author may judge the marketing cost too high. Mitigated because the honest version is still a strong claim (the design + the Act-I review are real) and because consistency with LIMITATIONS is itself a credibility asset for an integrity tool.

location.section: SKILL.md (description; also 'does NOT do' list and README 'will not do' / 'one hard rule')

quote:
RE-RUNS the analysis under an execution-provenance wall
  (no number enters the paper unless a logged re-run produced it)
issue: The 'no number enters the paper unless a logged re-run produced it' guarantee is asserted as an unconditional, present-tense product property in at least four places: the SKILL.md description (this quote), the SKILL.md 'What this skill does NOT do' list ('No number in the revised paper that a logged re-run did not produce.'), the README 'one hard rule' ('*no number enters your paper unless a real, logged re-run produced it.*'), and the README 'What it deliberately will not do' list. Two facts the paper itself states make this absolute oversized: (1) Act II has never been demonstrated end-to-end (LIMITATIONS: 'designed, demonstrated in part'), so the wall has never actually gated a real revised paper; and (2) the wall's enforcement is not what the absolute implies â€” LIMITATIONS concedes 'The "consistency" and "numeric-provenance" verifiers are LLM-audited, not deterministic scripts (only the quote-gate is a real script today).' An absolute guarantee ('no number ... unless') about a control that is (a) undemonstrated and (b) enforced by an LLM auditor, not a deterministic script, is sized beyond what the design can demonstrate today. The flat 'will not do' bullets are the worst offenders: they read as enforced-today guarantees with no tense hedge and no caveat.
why_it_matters: This is the provenance promise that an integrity-focused tool lives or dies on, and it is stated in the trigger-surface text (the SKILL.md description Claude itself reads to decide behavior) and in the unconditional 'will not do' lists. A user reads 'no number enters unless a logged re-run produced it' as a hard, currently-operative safety property; in fact it is an undemonstrated design whose numeric checks are themselves model-audited. Overstating the strength of a safety control is a correctness/integrity-class framing error under the rubric (a stated property that is not what the evidence supports), and it is exactly the property whose failure would let a fabricated number into a manuscript.
proposed_fix: Make the absolutes conditional on the design being a design, in every location they appear. In the 'will not do' / 'does NOT do' lists, change the bullet to scope it as an enforced *rule of the Act-II design* rather than a demonstrated outcome, e.g. 'Act II is built so that no number enters the revised paper unless a logged re-run produced it (the provenance rule; the numeric-provenance and consistency checks are LLM-audited today, not yet deterministic scripts â€” see LIMITATIONS.md).' At minimum, add the 'numeric checks are LLM-audited, not deterministic' caveat at the point of the SKILL.md description claim, since that surface currently carries no hedge.
risk_of_fix: Adding 'LLM-audited, not deterministic' to the description risks undercutting the one genuinely strong control (the deterministic quote-gate) by association, if a careless reader conflates the two; the fix must keep the quote-gate's deterministic status clearly separate. There is also a length cost in the description. Mitigated by keeping the quote-gate's 'real script' status explicit and only down-scoping the numeric/consistency wall.

location.section: SKILL.md (description; and README 'will not do' list) â€” no LIMITATIONS pointer at the claim

issue: The hedges that neutralize the Act-II overclaims (findings 001/002) exist ONLY in LIMITATIONS.md and are structurally severed from the surfaces that carry the claims. The SKILL.md description â€” the most-read surface and the text that triggers and configures the tool â€” asserts the strongest absolutes ('RE-RUNS the analysis ... no number enters the paper unless a logged re-run produced it') with no in-place caveat and no pointer to LIMITATIONS.md anywhere in SKILL.md (grep finds zero 'LIMITATIONS' references in the entire SKILL.md section). The README mentions LIMITATIONS once ('Honesty about limits.** See [`LIMITATIONS.md`]'), but that pointer sits in the 'where it fits' block and the no-measured-numbers paragraph â€” NOT at the point of the Act-II 'hands back a corrected, reproducing manuscript' claim (C-021) nor at the 'one hard rule' guarantee. A reader who reads the description, or the 'What it deliberately will not do' bullet list, and stops there (a normal reading path, especially since the description is what the agent harness consumes) never encounters the 'designed, demonstrated in part' / 'LLM-audited, not deterministic' qualifications. For an integrity tool whose own constitution demands 'Honest labeling ... never imply ... reproduction that did not happen,' burying the only reach-back to that honesty in a file the claim-surface never references is a self-inconsistency: the marketing surface implies a reproduction guarantee the LIMITATIONS file explicitly says has not happened.
why_it_matters: Whether an overclaim is fatal turns on whether a reasonable reader is actually reached by the correction. Here the strongest claims are on the surface most readers (and the triggering agent) see, and the corrective is in a file that surface never links. The hedge therefore does not, in practice, neutralize the marketing-surface claim â€” which is exactly the jurisdiction question. A LIMITATIONS file that is never cross-referenced from the claims it qualifies functions as deniability, not disclosure, and undercuts the tool's central trust proposition.
proposed_fix: Place a one-clause pointer at each strong claim: in the SKILL.md description after the Act-II sentence, add '(Act II is implemented, not yet demonstrated end-to-end; see LIMITATIONS.md)'; in both 'will not do' bullet lists, append 'â€” see LIMITATIONS.md for what is enforced vs. designed'; and add the LIMITATIONS link to the README 'bet 2' sentence, not only to the 'honesty about limits' block. The goal is that no path that surfaces the strong claim is more than one clause away from its qualifier.
risk_of_fix: Repeated 'see LIMITATIONS.md' pointers can clutter otherwise crisp marketing copy and, if overdone, make the tool read as defensive. Mitigated by using a single short parenthetical per claim rather than a paragraph, and by the fact that proximity of caveat to claim is standard honest-labeling practice.

location.section: SKILL.md (description)

quote:
reviews the paper
  to the sentence, every comment grounded in an exact quote (no fabrication, no
  confidence scores)
issue: Two universals here are oversized against what the design demonstrates by default. (1) 'reviews the paper to the sentence' implies per-sentence coverage as the standard behavior, but the paper's own Modes table and verification_panel.md make the sentence sweep a property only of the two heavy tiers (Symposium/Summit / exhaustive/monumental: 'close-reader sweeps return a verdict for **every** range'). The DEFAULT mode is Workshop, which has no per-sentence sweep â€” so 'reviews the paper to the sentence' is true for an opt-in heavy configuration, not for what a default run does. (2) 'every comment grounded in an exact quote' is contradicted by the paper's own first-class category of absence-silence findings, which grounding rule 9 explicitly defines as carrying NO quote ('their evidence *is* the absence ... exempt from the deterministic quote-gate'). By the tool's own design, not every comment is grounded in an exact quote; the highest-severity ones often are not. The universal 'every comment ... exact quote' overstates the grounding guarantee and, ironically, erases the absence-silence feature the constitution is proud of.
why_it_matters: Under the rubric this is a fixable overreach of a stated property (Medium): it materially mis-sizes two coverage/grounding guarantees that a careful referee or user would test. 'To the sentence' invites a user on the default tier to believe they got exhaustive per-sentence coverage they did not buy; 'every comment ... exact quote' invites the inference that an ungrounded comment is a malfunction, when the design intends ungrounded (absence) findings to exist. Neither moves the headline as hard as 001/002, but both are honesty-of-sizing defects in the same description sentence.
proposed_fix: Scope both universals. For coverage: 'reviews the paper down to the sentence in its exhaustive tiers' (or 'tile-by-tile, to the sentence at the deepest tiers'). For grounding: 'every *quotable* comment grounded in an exact quote, with absence/silence findings located by section instead' â€” which both stays true and showcases the absence-finding design rather than contradicting it.
risk_of_fix: The qualified version is longer and slightly less punchy in the description; 'every quotable comment' is a small hedge that a skim-reader might miss. Negligible scientific risk; the change only makes two existing guarantees accurate, and explicitly naming absence findings strengthens rather than weakens the pitch.

tradition: outsider / research-impact (does the contribution matter, and is its importance honestly sized?)

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md ("not yet proven") cross-read against SKILL.md description + README.md headline framing

quote: No measured effectiveness numbers yet.
issue: Strip away the machinery and ask the only question an outsider cares about: does this tool produce review that is actually better than the cheap alternatives, and does that matter to anyone? The manuscript answers, in its own words, that it does not know. It has "No measured effectiveness numbers yet," it instructs the reader to "treat the output as *one very thorough opinion*, not validated ground truth," and it calls a validation run "the single most important piece of future work." Meanwhile the headline framing sells exactly the opposite: "the largest possible Claude-only expert fleet," a tool that is "monumental," an epigraph promising "Every paper leaves changed." The entire claimed contribution is *trustworthy review at scale* — and the paper never demonstrates that the output is more correct, more complete, or more useful than a single AI pass or one of the lighter prior-art tools it concedes already exist. A 600-agent apparatus that catches the same things a one-shot reader would, or that confidently manufactures must-fix items at an unknown rate, would be an expensive way to feel rigorous. The paper cannot rule that world out, because it has measured nothing. The honesty of the LIMITATIONS section is real and it is the only thing keeping this from being a pure overclaim — but honesty about an unproven contribution does not make the contribution proven. As a research claim, "this matters" is asserted, not shown.
why_it_matters: Relevance is the load-bearing question for this artifact, and it is unanswered by the authors' own admission. Every other strength (grounding, the quote-gate, the provenance wall) governs *how* the review is produced, not *whether the produced review is worth having*. If a competent referee asked 'what changes in the world if this is exactly as described?', the manuscript offers no measured answer — only a promise that the answer is coming. The gap between the marketing register ('monumental', 'largest possible', 'every paper leaves changed') and the evidence register ('one very thorough opinion, not validated ground truth') is the central relevance defect.
proposed_fix: Resolve the framing one of two ways, and do it at the top, not only in LIMITATIONS. Either (a) demote the importance claims to match the evidence — lead the README/SKILL description with a single sentence stating no effectiveness has yet been measured and the tool is, today, 'one very thorough, well-grounded opinion', and reserve words like 'monumental' / 'largest possible fleet' until a recall/false-positive run exists; or (b) supply the missing evidence: run the planned validation on third-party papers with known or planted flaws, report recall and false-positive rate, and let those numbers — not adjectives — carry the importance claim. The authors already name (b) as their top roadmap item; the relevance finding is that until (b) lands, the prose must live within (a).
risk_of_fix: Toning down the headline framing risks under-selling genuinely careful engineering and could read as false modesty; over-correcting into pure hedging would bury the real design contribution (the grounded, debate-structured, provenance-walled architecture). The fix must rescope the *importance* claim without erasing the *design* claim. Adding a validation run risks the opposite outcome (the numbers may be unflattering), but that is the point of measuring.

tradition: outsider / research-impact (marginal value of the headline differentiator)

location.section: SKILL.md Modes table + README Modes table, read against LIMITATIONS.md 'Same-model decorrelation'

quote:
every seat is the same model class and can share a blind spot. A fleet's agreement is
  *not* independent corroboration.
issue: The single most prominent differentiator in the manuscript is scale: a modes table that climbs to '60-120+ expert seats' and '~300-600 agents', sold as the premium tier ('the most exhaustive pass'). The implicit relevance claim is that more seats buy you more trustworthy review. But the paper itself detonates that claim: because 'every seat is the same model class and can share a blind spot', 'A fleet's agreement is *not* independent corroboration.' If forty same-model seats agreeing is not corroboration, then the outsider's question — why does running 600 agents matter rather than 6? — has no answer in the text. The paper never argues the *marginal* value of scale: nowhere does it show (or even claim) that Symposium catches something Workshop misses, or that Summit's per-sentence sweep changes a single verdict relative to the default. The one mechanism that would convert agreement into genuine corroboration — the cross-provider 'what did we all miss?' dissent leg — is explicitly 'off-by-default' and optional. So the feature that would make scale matter is sidelined, and the scale that is foregrounded is, by the manuscript's own logic, of unproven marginal worth. An outsider is left suspecting that most of the agent count is theater: real cost, unproven incremental benefit.
why_it_matters: Scale is how this tool distinguishes itself from 'a single AI review' and from its own lighter modes; it is the relevance hook. A differentiator the paper concedes 'is not independent corroboration', and whose incremental value over the cheap default is never argued, cannot carry the importance claim. This is not a tone issue — it determines whether the premium modes have any reason to exist for a user, and whether the agent-count headline is meaningful or decorative.
proposed_fix: Make the marginal-value-of-scale argument explicit or stop foregrounding the agent count. Concretely: (i) state, per tier, what additional class of defect the larger fleet is expected to catch and why a same-model fleet of that size adds signal rather than correlated noise; (ii) if that case cannot yet be made, reframe the modes table around *coverage breadth* (more sentences/dimensions examined) rather than implying more *trust*, and say plainly that depth buys attention, not corroboration; and (iii) promote the cross-provider dissent leg to a first-class, on-by-recommendation option for high-stakes runs, since the manuscript itself identifies it as the only real corroboration mechanism. The authors already list (iii) on the roadmap; relevance demands it be elevated, because it is what would make the headline differentiator matter.
risk_of_fix: Reframing the modes table from 'trust' to 'attention/breadth' could make the premium tiers look less compelling commercially; that is an honest cost. Turning the cross-provider leg on by default conflicts with the deliberate 'Claude-only by design' positioning and with the privacy/no-train constraints the manuscript flags, so it must be opt-in-but-recommended, not forced. Care needed so the rescope does not contradict the (separately defensible) claim that breadth of examination has value.

location.section: SKILL.md/README Modes tables and 'What makes it trustworthy at scale' — no cost/benefit argument anywhere

issue: The manuscript quantifies *cost* vividly — up to '~300-600 agents' per run, runs that 'can run for a while by design', a per-section sentence sweep whose cost 'also scales with paper length' — but never once weighs that cost against a benefit. For whom, and for which decision, is a 600-agent run worth its time, money, and token burn rather than a 20-agent Roundtable or a single careful read? The paper states who the user is ('researchers who want more than a list of complaints') and when it nominally helps ('when you want the argument *and* the rebuild'), but it never argues that the *importance* of the output justifies the *magnitude* of the spend — especially given (per GEN-REL-01) that the output's effectiveness is unmeasured and (per GEN-REL-02) that the extra agents may not be corroborating anything. An outsider reads this as a tool whose costs are concrete and whose payoff is asserted. The 'so what for practice' is never sized: there is no statement of the stakes at which this apparatus pays off versus the stakes at which a cheaper tool is the rational choice.
why_it_matters: Practical relevance is a cost-benefit judgment, and a paper proposing an expensive instrument owes the reader the conditions under which the expense is justified. Omitting it leaves the central practical claim — that this is worth running — unfalsifiable and unargued. This is a first-class absence finding: the evidence is the silence. It is fixable (state the decision-stakes threshold) and therefore not alone fatal, but it is exactly the question the generalist seat exists to force.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit 'when is this worth it' statement tying mode to stakes: e.g., specify that the heavy tiers are intended for high-stakes submissions where the cost of a missed flaw dominates compute cost (a flagship-journal submission, a high-consequence policy paper), and that for routine drafts the lighter modes or a single pass are the rational choice. Pair each mode in the table with an honest cost descriptor (rough agent-run count / expected wall-clock) and a one-line 'use this when ...'. This converts the abstract 'pick your depth' into an argued cost-benefit the reader can act on, and it is consistent with the existing honesty about limits.
risk_of_fix: Naming concrete cost figures invites pushback if real-world costs vary widely across plans and paper lengths, so the descriptors must be ranges flagged as approximate. Stating that cheaper modes suffice for routine drafts may cannibalize use of the premium tiers — an honest cost the paper should accept rather than obscure.

A strong scientist one field over has no model of what one 'agent' IS: a separate process? an isolated LLM context? a prompt invocation? a dollar of compute? location.section: SKILL.md 'Modes' (cost model)

location.section: Whole document (SKILL.md + README.md + LIMITATIONS.md); no single thesis statement

issue: Read as a paper, the document never states, in one place, a single declarative thesis an outsider can grasp and test: what problem, what is the claimed contribution, and what would make it true or false. Instead the 'contribution' is diffused across a SKILL.md front-matter blurb, a README marketing section ('What it does that a single AI review doesn't' — which presumes the reader already knows the baseline), and a LIMITATIONS file. The genre itself is ambiguous to an outsider — research paper, software README, or product brochure? — and the epigraph 'Every paper leaves changed.' substitutes a slogan for a thesis. A strong scientist from another field finishes the document able to recite features but unable to state, in one sentence, 'the claim of this work is X.'
why_it_matters: If a reviewer cannot locate the thesis, they cannot judge whether the evidence supports it — and an outsider, who is exactly the audience the paper says it serves, is left assembling the claim themselves. A buried thesis is a first-order comprehension failure, not a polish issue.
proposed_fix: Add a single explicit thesis/contribution paragraph near the top (before features): one sentence on the problem (AI paper-review either debates OR fixes, rarely both, and rarely with verified grounding at scale), one on the claimed contribution, and one on what is and is not yet demonstrated — written so an outsider can restate it.
risk_of_fix: Compressing the contribution into one paragraph risks overclaiming by omission of the very caveats the LIMITATIONS file carefully states; the new paragraph must carry the 'not yet validated' qualifier or it will read as a stronger claim than the authors intend.

location.section: SKILL.md/README.md (TRIBUNAL/ATELIER, dual name), prompts (Scout, Runner/Scribe)

quote:
**One skill, said two ways.** `paper-workshop` is the repo you install and the phrase you
> type to run it; **CRUCIBLE** is its name
issue: The reader must carry a stack of proper-noun codenames that map onto plain concepts: the tool has two names (paper-workshop AND CRUCIBLE — the paper itself stops to explain the collision, a tell that it is a known friction), the two acts are TRIBUNAL and ATELIER, and the roles are the Scout, the Runner, and the Scribe. None of these codenames adds information an outsider needs; each is a lookup the reader must maintain. ATELIER in particular ('a workshop/studio', French) is opaque to many non-native readers and adds nothing over 'the rebuild phase'.
why_it_matters: Gratuitous codenames raise working-memory load and slow an outsider's first read with no compensating clarity. When a document must pause to disambiguate its own product name, that is evidence the naming is impeding, not aiding, comprehension.
proposed_fix: Lead with the plain function and demote the codename to a parenthetical on first mention, then prefer the plain term: 'Act I (review)' / 'Act II (rebuild)' instead of TRIBUNAL/ATELIER; pick ONE primary product name and gloss the other once. Keep codenames for flavor in headers only.
risk_of_fix: The codenames are also the branding; stripping them entirely could conflict with the authors' product identity. The fix is to subordinate, not delete — over-aggressive removal would fight the intended brand.

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md (Act II integrity angle)

quote: Does the edit suppress/attenuate a result, narrow a sample, drop a control/observation, weaken a caveat, swap the headline spec, or HARK?
issue: 'HARK' is dropped with no expansion. It is a discipline-specific acronym (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) from the psychology/methodology literature; a strong physicist, biologist, or mathematician will not recognize it. It appears in a hard-gate integrity check — i.e. a load-bearing place — yet a whole class of readers cannot parse what the gate is guarding against. This is one instance of a broader pattern: 'commit-and-reveal' (mechanism-design term), 'steelman' (rationalist-discourse term), 'N correlated draws' (statistics shorthand) are all used without gloss.
why_it_matters: An integrity gate the reader cannot decode is an integrity gate the reader cannot trust or audit. For a tool whose entire value proposition is auditable rigor, an undefined term inside the rigor machinery directly undercuts the outsider's ability to evaluate the safeguard.
proposed_fix: Expand on first use: 'or HARK (hypothesizing after results are known — silently recasting an exploratory finding as if it had been predicted)'. Do the same one-time gloss for 'steelman', 'commit-and-reveal', and 'correlated draws'.
risk_of_fix: Low; the only risk is a gloss that subtly misdefines the term (e.g. conflating HARKing with p-hacking). The parenthetical must be accurate to the methodological meaning.

location.section: helpers/orchestration.md (Step 7) + helpers/verification_panel.md

quote: It triages each finding into lanes A/B/C/D
issue: The Act-II machinery introduces two parallel undefined taxonomies the outsider cannot decode: 'lanes A/B/C/D' (the labels A-D are never spelled out where they are introduced) and 'edit_class' values ('presentation', 'additive-verified', 'numeric', 'result-suppressing', 'claim-altering'). The reader is told auto-apply happens 'only if edit_class is presentation or additive-verified' and that 'lane-C/D proposals' wait for sign-off — but is never given the legend mapping A/B/C/D to anything, so the central safety rule (what auto-applies vs. what waits for a human) is stated in a private code.
why_it_matters: The auto-apply boundary is the single most safety-relevant rule in Act II (it determines what the tool can change without asking). Expressing it in undefined lane letters means an outsider literally cannot verify the safety claim they are being asked to trust.
proposed_fix: Give the lane legend at first mention (e.g. 'Lane A = presentation-only auto-apply; B = additive/verified auto-apply; C = numeric, author sign-off; D = claim-altering, author sign-off') and state the auto-apply rule once in plain words, not only via edit_class tokens.

location.section: SKILL.md Modes table vs README.md Modes table

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md rule 13 + README/SKILL

tradition: Outsider empiricist (a results-per-dollar field one door over: applied econometrics / experimental science)

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md (“not yet proven”); README.md (“Honesty about limits”)

quote: No measured effectiveness numbers yet.
issue: Step back from the machinery and ask the only question an outsider cares about: does this fleet actually catch flaws a cheap reviewer misses, and does it avoid manufacturing confident wrong ones? The paper's answer, in its own words, is that nobody has measured it — “treat the output as *one very thorough opinion*, not validated ground truth” and a measured recall/false-positive run is conceded to be “the single most important piece of future work.” The entire claimed contribution (a 45–600-agent debating tribunal that finds real problems) rests on an effect size that has never been observed. For any neighboring evidence-based field, that is the textbook definition of “cannot tell whether it matters”: every internal rail can be real and the headline benefit still be zero.
why_it_matters: Significance is unestablished, not merely unproven-in-detail. A reader from another field has no basis to believe a 300–600-agent run delivers anything a single careful pass does not. The honest disclosure is to the authors' credit, but disclosure of a missing result does not supply the result — the so-what remains unsupported.
proposed_fix: Lead with a small measured validation — run the tool on a handful of third-party papers with known or planted flaws and report recall and false-positive rate, even if n is tiny and labeled illustrative. Until that exists, demote every “monumental / most exhaustive / examines everything” significance claim to a capability description and state explicitly in the abstract that effectiveness is undemonstrated.
risk_of_fix: A tiny or self-selected validation set could itself be over-read as proof; the fix must carry the same “illustrative, not decisive” humility the authors already apply to the n=5 comparison, or it trades one overclaim for another.

location.section: README.md (“Where it fits”) and Modes table; SKILL.md Modes table

quote:
If you only want a fast referee-style critique, lighter tools (and CRUCIBLE's own **Desk
Review** mode) do that. CRUCIBLE earns its keep when you want the argument *and* the rebuild.
issue: The headline differentiator is scale-plus-debate: a fleet that grows from ~1 to ~600 agents, every contested claim argued by rival schools. But the paper never demonstrates — or even claims to have measured — that the heavy modes find anything the trivial baseline misses. It concedes its own Desk Review (“a few lenses,” ~1–6 agents) already does “a fast referee-style critique,” yet offers no head-to-head showing what the extra 40–600 agents buy. The crucial outsider comparison — N-agent tribunal vs. one careful Claude pass vs. one competent human referee — is simply absent. Without it, the scaling story (the paper's central selling point) has an undefined payoff: more compute is an input cost, not a demonstrated benefit.
why_it_matters: A neighboring field rewards marginal value over the cheap alternative, not headcount. If Workshop/Symposium/Summit do not measurably beat Desk Review or a single referee, the contribution collapses to “a well-engineered single AI review with extra steps,” which the README itself admits “lighter tools” already provide. The importance claim cannot be evaluated because the only comparison that would establish it is never made.
proposed_fix: Add a baseline-contrast experiment: run Desk Review, one heavy mode, and (ideally) a human referee on the same paper(s) and report what the heavy mode caught that the baseline did not (and what it falsely flagged). Frame the contribution as the *delta over baseline*, not as fleet size or exhaustiveness.
risk_of_fix: If the delta turns out small, the paper's central pitch weakens — but discovering that is the point; suppressing the comparison to protect the pitch would be the worse error. A single-paper contrast also risks cherry-picking, so the predicate (which papers, how flaws are scored) must be fixed in advance.

location.section: README.md (“The panel is built from your paper”); examples/self-audit; LIMITATIONS.md

quote: A self-audit is a development pass, not independent validation.
issue: The tool's reach is sold on a mechanism: a scout that assembles experts specific to “your identification strategy, your estimator, publication bias, your benchmark, your proof” — i.e., it claims to travel across econometrics, machine learning, and mathematics. Yet the only run exhibited anywhere is the tool reviewing its own design documents (this very prose), which the authors correctly label a closed-loop development pass. There is no demonstration on a real quantitative paper in any neighboring field — no econometrics manuscript, no ML benchmark paper, no proof. So the cross-field generalizability that is the whole point of a “topic-adapted fleet” is asserted by construction and shown nowhere. An outsider in economics or biology has zero evidence the adaptation fires correctly on a paper from their world.
why_it_matters: “Works on its own README” is the weakest possible evidence of cross-domain reach, because the README is not a quantitative paper and the reviewer wrote the thing it reviewed. The breadth claim that makes the tool interesting beyond the AI-agents niche is unsupported by any out-of-distribution example.
proposed_fix: Show at least one end-to-end run on a real third-party paper from a quantitative field (with the roster the scout built and the findings it produced), clearly labeled illustrative. One concrete out-of-domain example does more for the travel claim than the entire mechanism description.
risk_of_fix: A single showcased paper invites cherry-picking and could over-generalize from one success; it must be presented as an existence proof of the workflow, not as evidence of accuracy, to stay inside the paper's own honesty constraints.

tradition: Outsider empiricist (weight-of-evidence on a design-justifying result)

location.section: README.md (“Lineage”)

quote:
n = 5 meta-analyses, found a Claude-only
configuration ranked above its cross-model setup by an independent judge
issue: The one quantitative result offered to justify the load-bearing design choice (“Claude-only by design”) is not even about this tool — it is borrowed from a predecessor, n=5, one run per arm. Checked against the fetched predecessor README, the lone “independent judge” was specifically Gemini (a single model with, in the source's own words, “its own biases”), the result was a 3-way comparison compressed to “ranked above its cross-model setup,” and the paper drops two caveats the source itself flags: that blinding was imperfect so “part of the gap is presentation, not reasoning,” and that on three of the five papers the rival arm's raw files were lost to an encoding fault and re-run. proposed_fix: When invoking the n=5 result, name the judge (Gemini), state it was a 3-way comparison, and carry over the source's own “presentation, not reasoning” and lost-raw-files caveats — or drop the result to a one-line pointer and stop leaning on it to justify the design. Verified against the staged source note for s168.
risk_of_fix: Fully surfacing the caveats further weakens an already-weak empirical leg, which may leave the “Claude-only” choice looking unjustified — but that is the honest state, and the paper elsewhere commits to exactly this candor.

location.section: SKILL.md (description, “Use mad-research instead…”)

quote: the largest possible Claude-only expert fleet
issue: Across the manuscript the contribution is repeatedly framed by *size and exhaustiveness* — “largest possible Claude-only expert fleet,” “the most exhaustive pass,” “300–600-agent run,” “examines everything.” From outside the AI-agents conversation this reads as optimizing the wrong variable: agent count and pass-exhaustiveness are inputs the user pays for, not outcomes a scientific field values. A neighboring discipline does not ask “how many reviewers did you simulate?” — it asks “what true defect did you find that I would have shipped, and how often are you wrong?” By foregrounding fleet scale as the headline virtue, the paper risks landing as impressive engineering within a narrow niche rather than as a result that matters to science broadly.
why_it_matters: Framing the contribution around scale invites the outsider's verdict “competent within a narrow conversation” rather than “important.” The genuinely cross-field-significant claims here (deterministic quote-grounding, the execution-provenance wall against fabricated numbers) are arguably more transportable and are under-sold relative to headcount.
proposed_fix: Re-center the framing on outcomes and on the transportable integrity mechanisms (quote-gate, provenance wall, tone-invariant severity) rather than fleet size; present scale as a cost dial, not the contribution. Reserve “monumental/exhaustive” for after an effectiveness number exists.
risk_of_fix: Down-weighting the scale framing removes the most striking selling point and could make the tool sound more modest than the authors wish; but modesty calibrated to the evidence is the correct trade for cross-field credibility.

tradition: Outsider empiricist (does the differentiating half of the value proposition exist yet)

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md (“Act II's reproduction check needs a precise predicate”)

quote:
treat Act II as *designed, demonstrated in
part*
issue: The paper's stated reason-to-exist over lighter tools is the rebuild: “CRUCIBLE earns its keep when you want the argument *and* the rebuild,” the part that “re-runs your analysis and hands back a corrected, reproducing manuscript.” But Act II — precisely that differentiating half — is conceded to be only “designed, demonstrated in part,” with the reproduction predicate (tolerances, seeds, environment) not yet shipped and never shown end-to-end on a real paper. An outsider deciding whether to care is left with a promise, not a demonstration, on the decisive feature.

risk_of_fix: Labeling the differentiator undemonstrated weakens the headline pitch and may make the tool look like the lighter reviewers it distinguishes itself from — but that is the current evidential reality the LIMITATIONS file already half-concedes.

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md / SKILL.md / README.md

quote: We have not yet published a run on third-party papers with known/planted flaws scoring **recall** (does it catch the real flaws?) and **false-positive rate** (does it manufacture confident wrong "must-fix" items?).
issue: This paper dies because it ships and markets a research-INTEGRITY instrument whose one load-bearing empirical claim — that it catches real flaws without manufacturing false ones — was never measured even once, and the paper says so in its own LIMITATIONS while shipping anyway; the instructive death is a CRUCIBLE-'workshopped' manuscript that gets a confident verdict, is published, and is retracted for a flaw that sat inside a range the tool certified as 'covered', at which point the indictment writes itself from the tool's own documentation.
why_it_matters: Recall and false-positive rate are the only two numbers that establish whether the entire apparatus (300-600 agents, rival traditions, a verification panel) does the job it claims or merely performs rigor convincingly. A tool for catching errors that has never been measured for whether it catches errors — or invents them — has zero demonstrated validity; every other claim in the paper is downstream of this gap. A reviewer at any methods venue rejects on this point alone, and a deployed-then-embarrassed failure is the predictable consequence of releasing it before the measurement exists.
proposed_fix: Do not present CRUCIBLE as a usable integrity tool until the validation run exists: run it on a held-out corpus of third-party papers with known/planted flaws, report measured recall and false-positive rate with CIs, and reframe the entire contribution as 'a designed-and-engineered system, validation pending' rather than a working reviewer. If the number cannot be produced before submission, the honest paper is a systems/design paper that explicitly disclaims effectiveness in the abstract, not the README's 'sharpest objection a top referee would raise ... and the actual edits that answer it.'
risk_of_fix: Reframing to 'validation pending' substantially deflates the contribution and may push the paper below the bar of the target venue — but shipping an unmeasured integrity tool with confident framing is the failure mode being pre-mortem'd, so the deflation is the correct, survivable outcome.

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md

quote:
Until
  that exists, treat the output as *one very thorough opinion*, not validated ground truth.
  This is the single most important piece of future work.
issue: The paper concedes the single most important piece of evidence does not exist and is 'future work', yet the SKILL.md/README/title still sell the system in the present tense as an operating referee fleet — a referee will read this concession as the author rejecting their own paper, and rank it a desk-reject for a tool whose central efficacy claim is admittedly unestablished.
why_it_matters: A paper that names its own missing keystone as 'the single most important piece of future work' and then submits without it is asking the referee to accept the thesis on faith. The gap between 'one very thorough opinion' (the honest internal description) and the marketing surface ('the sharpest objection a top referee would raise') is exactly the credibility gap that produces either desk-rejection or, post-publication, a humiliating 'they admitted they never tested it' takedown.
proposed_fix: Promote the LIMITATIONS concession into the abstract and contribution statement verbatim ('treat the output as one very thorough opinion, not validated ground truth') so the present-tense efficacy framing elsewhere cannot contradict it; better, hold submission until roadmap item 1 (the validation run) is done and leads the paper, as the roadmap itself proposes ('lead the README with the number').
risk_of_fix: Surfacing the disclaimer in the abstract makes the modest evidentiary state unmissable and may itself trigger desk-rejection — but that is strictly better than the same rejection arriving after a referee discovers the buried concession, or after a public failure.

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md / SKILL.md

quote:
but every seat is the same model class and can share a blind spot. A fleet's agreement is
  *not* independent corroboration.
issue: The headline selling point — 'the largest possible Claude-only expert fleet' (SKILL.md) of up to 300-600 agents — is, by the paper's own admission, a population of correlated draws from one model that can share a blind spot, so the marquee scale is precisely the axis along which the tool fails silently; the paper dies the day a reviewer notes that 'the largest possible fleet' and 'a fleet's agreement is not independent corroboration' are the same sentence read two ways.
why_it_matters: Scale is the paper's central visible promise and its pricing of seriousness (Summit = 300-600 agents = 'the most exhaustive pass'). If N same-model agents are correlated, adding agents buys diminishing real coverage while inflating the appearance of thoroughness — the worst possible property for an integrity tool, because it manufactures confidence without manufacturing correctness. A correlated blind spot is exactly the mechanism by which a CRUCIBLE-blessed paper gets retracted: the whole fleet missed the same thing, and the coverage certificate said 'examined'.
proposed_fix: Stop advertising raw agent count as the headline virtue; demote scale to a secondary knob and lead with the decorrelation evidence. Make the cross-provider 'what did we all miss?' leg ON by default (it is currently 'off-by-default'), or empirically show that marginal same-model agents add non-redundant findings (a saturation curve) so the 300-600 figure is justified rather than theatrical.
risk_of_fix: Turning the external leg on by default breaks the 'Claude-only' identity the paper repeatedly markets and adds cost/configuration burden; demoting scale weakens the most legible differentiator from a single AI review. The mitigation is real engineering and framing work, not a one-line edit.

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md

quote:
until that ships
  and is demonstrated end-to-end on a real paper, treat Act II as *designed, demonstrated in
  part* â€” and re-derive any number yourself before trusting it.
issue: Act II — the half of the contribution that the README claims sets CRUCIBLE apart ('an integrated rebuild that re-runs your analysis and hands back a corrected, reproducing manuscript') — is by the paper's own words only 'designed, demonstrated in part' and carries the instruction to 're-derive any number yourself before trusting it', which is a confession that the rebuild's core guarantee has never been shown to hold on a real paper; the paper dies when a referee asks for one end-to-end worked example and there is none.
why_it_matters: The Execution-Provenance Wall ('no number enters the paper unless a real, logged re-run produced it') is sold as the feature that makes the rebuild trustworthy, but a guarantee that has never been exercised end-to-end on a real manuscript is a design diagram, not a result. 'Re-derive any number yourself' negates the entire value proposition of an automated rebuild. A second act that asks the user to redo its work by hand cannot anchor a paper claiming it 'rebuilds the paper — it doesn't just review it.'
proposed_fix: Either (a) demonstrate Act II end-to-end on at least one real, third-party paper with a precise per-artifact reproduction predicate (tolerances, seeds, environment capture) and report it, or (b) cut Act II from the contribution claims and present it explicitly as roadmap/prototype, removing 'rebuilds ... reproducing manuscript' from the framing until the demonstration exists.
risk_of_fix: Cutting Act II removes one of the two pillars the paper uses to distinguish itself ('the combination two of them rarely make together'), collapsing the novelty claim toward 'reviewers that debate' alone; demonstrating it properly is substantial work that may not fit the submission timeline.

location.section: LIMITATIONS.md / coverage_rubric.md

quote:
**Coverage means attention, not correctness.** The sentence-coverage ledger certifies every
  range was *examined*, not that each was *correctly* reviewed; a flaw can hide in a
  "covered" range.
issue: The 'completeness certificate' and the claim that the tool 'examined everything' rest on a coverage notion the paper itself defines as attention-not-correctness, where 'a flaw can hide in a covered range' — so the most authoritative-sounding deliverable (a certificate that every sentence was covered) certifies nothing about whether anything was caught; the paper dies the day a published, CRUCIBLE-certified manuscript is shown to contain a fatal flaw inside a 'covered' sentence and a critic quotes this exact admission back as 'they knew the certificate was hollow.'
why_it_matters: A 'completeness certificate' is the kind of artifact users will wave at editors and co-authors as evidence of diligence. If it certifies attention, not correctness, it is liable to be read — by exactly the non-expert audience the tool courts — as a clean bill of health it cannot be. The reputational failure is not a subtle methods point; it is a certificate-shaped object that invites misreading, and the misreading is what gets the paper publicly embarrassed.
proposed_fix: Rename the artifact away from 'certificate' (e.g. 'attention ledger' or 'examination log') and stamp every instance of it with the disclaimer 'examined, not validated; a flaw can hide here'; strike or heavily qualify any phrasing implying the tool 'examined everything' in a way a reader could equate with 'found everything'.
risk_of_fix: Renaming and disclaiming the certificate reduces the persuasive weight of a flagship deliverable and the 'we examined everything' selling point; some users specifically want the certificate as social proof, and weakening it lowers perceived value.

location.section: SKILL.md / rubric.md / helpers/verification_panel.md

issue: The paper specifies, in elaborate detail, the failure mode of a confident WRONG must-fix (the false positive), but never characterizes or bounds the inverse and more dangerous failure — a confident GREEN LIGHT on a paper that is actually fatally flawed (a false negative / miss) — even though that is the exact event that produces the 'published then retracted' embarrassment the tool is supposed to prevent; nowhere does the manuscript state what happens, or what the user is owed, when the fleet converges on 'competitive' and is wrong.
why_it_matters: For an integrity tool, the catastrophic error is not crying wolf, it is blessing a flawed paper that then fails publicly. The whole document optimizes against, and measures (in the roadmap), false positives ('manufacture confident wrong must-fix items'), while the symmetric false-negative — the missed fatal flaw — has no metric, no bound, and no user-facing warning attached to a clean verdict. A user who receives 'competitive' will reasonably treat it as reassurance; the paper never tells them it cannot be. The omission is the seed of the worst-case death: the tool said go, the paper went, the field saw it break.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit, prominent treatment of the false-negative (missed-flaw) risk: state that a clean/competitive verdict is NOT a guarantee of soundness, measure recall (the miss rate) as a first-class number in the validation run, and attach a standing disclaimer to every positive verdict that the absence of found flaws is not evidence of their absence.
risk_of_fix: Foregrounding the miss-rate and disclaiming positive verdicts directly undercuts the product's reassurance value and the 'serious pre-submission review' positioning; honestly, it makes the tool sound less like a safety net, which is the accurate but commercially deflating message.
